payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Put a frog in the toilet
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Is a recognizable frog visible in the toilet bowl opening or directly at its rim?
node.criteria: Pass if a recognizable frog is visible within the bowl opening or directly at its rim. Fail if that region is assessable and contains no recognizable frog. Unknown if frog identity or visibility of that region is insufficient. Identify the candidate and its visible location; this check does not establish that the frog is inside the bowl or that the request is complete.
node.binding: Inspect the edited image using the source toilet as the reference. Distinguish the bowl opening and rim from the raised lid, tank, surrounding fixtures, and floor. Frogs exclusively on those other surfaces do not pass this check.

node_traces.evidence: A recognizable green frog is visible inside the toilet bowl opening, resting on the inner bowl. Other frogs appear on the raised lid, tank area, and floor, but the bowl frog satisfies this check.
A recognizable green frog is visible inside the toilet bowl opening, resting within the rim. Other frogs appear on the raised lid and floor, but the bowl frog alone satisfies this check.

fulfillment: The node’s binding asks only whether a frog is inside the bowl, so it collapses the rubric’s distinct progress and completion criteria into a binary placement test. The edited image does show a frog in the bowl, but the source already contains a small object in the bowl and the edit adds several conspicuous frogs on unrelated surfaces; the traces’ repeated “added requested placement” claims do not establish that the requested bowl placement is complete. Preserve the ordered evidence roles: use s1 to identify a candidate, s2 to compare source and edit for requested progress, and s3 to assess whether that candidate is actually inside the bowl; do not count dependent observations as independent corroboration. Make the completion criterion distinguish a completed placement from visible but incomplete progress, and reserve unknown for unresolved or conflicting evidence. The five identical high-confidence “yes” outcomes despite a partial reference suggest a systematic criterion/binding mismatch, not a transport or dependency failure; investigate that mismatch rather than lowering confidence or treating repetition as proof.
s3: The binding reduces this support node to a binary interior-placement test, so it can pass even when the overall edit is only partial. Keep s3’s narrow geometric role—independently assess whether the identified candidate is actually in the bowl, using the rim and cavity rather than 2-D overlap—but make its evidence explicitly distinguish that finding from completion of the requested edit. The source already has a small object in the bowl; the edit adds a frog there, while other frogs are on the lid and floor. Treat s2’s source comparison as the progress evidence and do not let s3’s pass, or repeated dependent descriptions of the same frog, imply that all requested changes are complete. Preserve the ordered s1→s2→s3 evidence roles and use unknown only for genuinely unresolved geometry. The repeated high-confidence yes outcomes point to a criterion/binding mismatch, not a transport or dependency failure; investigate that mismatch rather than lowering confidence or forcing a label from the reference.
s2: The binding already assigns s2 the right role—compare source and edit for requested progress—so avoid changing it into a completion test or making it responsible for s3’s geometric judgment. The traces repeatedly call the bowl frog “added” and pass with high confidence, but the source image already contains a small object in the bowl; the edit visibly adds a frog there, as well as frogs on the lid and floor. Require the comparison to distinguish the pre-existing bowl object from the newly added frog and to ground progress in that specific change, not merely in a frog’s presence or repeated descriptions of the same candidate. Keep unrelated placements from counting as requested progress. Preserve the ordered s1→s2→s3 roles and use unknown only when the comparison or relevant spatial evidence is genuinely unresolved. The partial aggregate label is a diagnostic signal, not atomic ground truth: investigate whether the node’s pass is being mapped to overall completion downstream, rather than forcing s2 to fail or weakening its progress criterion. Traces show valid, queried executions and no transport or dependency failure; the mismatch is semantic/criterion or outcome-routing related, not a reason to lower confidence.
